items.title: Eyes have evolved independently more than 40 times
items.claim: Eyes are complicated. Darwin worried about them in Origin of Species. Modern phylogenetics shows that eyes — from basic photoreceptors to full image-forming structures — have evolved independently somewhere between 40 and 60 times across animal lineages.
items.prompt: What does this tell us about evolution?

options.text: Eyes are too complex to evolve once, let alone many times

Photoreception is selected for so strongly that wherever a workable starting point exists (a light-sensitive protein) selection assembles eyes; complex outcomes evolve repeatedly when the gradient of advantage is steep
All eyes descend from a single ancestor
Vision is impossible without divine design

items.reveal_title: Eyes as evolutionary stress-tests for gradualism
items.reveal:
Modern eyes include: vertebrate camera eyes, cephalopod camera eyes (independently evolved, no blind spot), trilobite calcite-lens compound eyes, scallop mirror eyes, copepod parabolic-reflector eyes, jumping-spider sharp-focus eyes, brittle-star whole-body lensed skin.

Nilsson and Pelger (1994) modelled the evolution of a vertebrate-style camera eye from a flat patch of photoreceptors. With realistic mutation rates and selection coefficients of 1 percent, they estimated 400,000 generations — about half a million years — to produce a fully functional eye.

The common element across all 40+ origins: opsin proteins. The receptor molecules are conserved; the architectures around them have been built and rebuilt many times.
items.why: Eyes feel like such complex organs that they 'must' be hard to evolve. They are exactly the kind of thing selection invents many times when given a good starting molecule.

items.title: Lakes flip between two stable states with no warning
items.claim: A clear lake with submerged plants can — if nutrient loading exceeds a threshold — suddenly transform into a green, turbid lake dominated by algae. The shift is rapid, hard to reverse, and almost impossible to predict from gradual measurements.
items.prompt: What's happening at the tipping point?

options.text: Positive feedback loops (algae shade out plants; sediment resuspends; phosphorus releases from anoxic sediments) take over once a threshold is crossed; the new state then reinforces itself

items.reveal_title: Marten Scheffer and alternative stable states
items.reveal:
Marten Scheffer and colleagues (Nature 2001, 2009) formalised the concept of alternative stable states in ecology. Many ecosystems can sit in one of two (or more) regimes, with sharp transitions between them.

A shallow lake's clear regime: rooted plants stabilise sediment; light penetrates; zooplankton eat algae. The turbid regime: algae bloom; light is blocked; plants die; bottom-feeding fish stir up sediment; phosphorus releases from anoxic mud; algae get more nutrient. Each state reinforces itself.

Loading a clear lake with phosphorus may have NO obvious effect — until a threshold is crossed. Then it flips fast. Reducing phosphorus AFTER the flip rarely restores the clear state directly; the lake stays turbid because the turbid state's feedback loops are now in charge. You may need to remove fish, biomanipulate, or wait years.

Similar regime shifts: coral reef to algal mat, savannah to desert (Sahara, 5500 BC), tundra to forest.

Early-warning signals (slowing recovery from perturbations, rising variance) precede tipping points by months to decades, but are subtle and contested.
items.why: Slow change feels safe. Real ecosystems can absorb stress invisibly for years and then collapse to a new state in months. The signal you want comes after the threshold is crossed.

items.title: Your muscles cannot share their sugar reserves with your brain
items.claim: Your body stores carbohydrate as glycogen. The liver holds ~100 grams; skeletal muscle ~400 grams. The liver's glycogen feeds the blood and brain. Muscle glycogen is for muscle's own use — it cannot release glucose to the bloodstream.
items.prompt: Why can the liver release glucose to blood but muscle cannot?

options.text: Muscle is too far from blood vessels

Liver expresses glucose-6-phosphatase, the enzyme that removes the phosphate from glucose-6-phosphate so glucose can leave the cell; skeletal muscle does not have this enzyme, so the breakdown product is trapped and used locally

items.reveal:
Glycogen breakdown:
1. Glycogen phosphorylase clips glucose-1-phosphate off the glycogen chain.
2. Phosphoglucomutase converts it to glucose-6-phosphate.
3. To leave the cell, the phosphate must be removed (glucose can cross membranes, but glucose-6-phosphate cannot).

Liver and kidney have glucose-6-phosphatase — they CAN remove the phosphate and export free glucose into the blood, supplying the brain and red blood cells.

Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase. The glucose-6-phosphate must be used locally — typically immediately entering glycolysis for ATP production.

The Cori cycle compensates indirectly: muscle generates lactate (during anaerobic exertion), exports it to the liver, where it's converted back to glucose (gluconeogenesis) and shipped back to muscle.

Von Gierke's disease (glycogen storage disease type I) is an inherited deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase: even liver glycogen cannot be exported. Patients have severe fasting hypoglycaemia.

Liver glycogen depletes in ~24 hours of fasting; muscle glycogen depletes in ~90 minutes of hard exercise. After that, fat and (eventually) protein become the energy source.
items.why: Sugar storage feels like a shared pool. It isn't — the body has specialised tissue-level energy compartments, controlled by which enzymes each tissue expresses.
